paragraphs.notes: Butler's 'made sure' is the dead sense 'felt certain' (Od. 9.496 καὶ δὴ φάμεν αὐτόθ᾽ ὀλέσθαι, 'we thought we were lost then and there'). Read today it means 'ensured', so the men seem to say they ensured their own deaths. 'felt sure' is Butler's own phrase for this sense (PG #1727 line 9799, 'he felt sure it was Minerva', checked in the pinned source), so the edit is a D29 restoration, not a paraphrase. 'sure', 'had been' and 'the death of us' are kept. The packet's consistency worry is settled: the final list also changes 4.54 and 4.57 to 'had felt sure' (B04-03, B04-04), and none of Butler's eight 'made sure' survives in the AFTER. 13.28, 16.3 and 17.3 print 'was sure', 16.31 'were sure' and 20.0 'thought you were doomed'. The remaining 'make sure' at 4.43, 13.2 and 16.34 is the current 'ensure' sense and correct. Butler ¶36 has no 'felt', so there is no collision. Punctuation is untouched.

Kin sense confirmed. Od. 9.532 φίλους τ᾽ ἰδέειν καὶ ἱκέσθαι οἶκον ἐϋκτίμενον ('to see his dear ones and reach his well-built house') uses the same formula (φίλους τ᾽ ἰδέειν καὶ ἱκέσθαι) as 7.76 (7.7 here), which the Book 7 blind reader flagged. 'loved ones' is the current, register-neutral word for φίλοι in this sense. The AFTER carries it at all eight formula sites (1.4, 2.23, 4.39, 5.3, 5.8, 7.7, 7.12, 9.40; checked). Butler's nearest other 'friends' are not the formula: 8.6 and 8.16 'tell his friends' on his return, 23.11, and 24.10 'our friends at home'. His Nausicaa line (6.22, Od. 6.314-315) has no 'friends' ('you may hope to see your own country again'), so the rule's list is complete. The rest of the curse is untouched: never reach home alive, late, in sore plight, after losing all his men, in another man's ship, trouble in his house. Neither Butler ¶40 nor the AFTER has 'love' or 'dear', so there is no collision.
